spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The decisive move is to stop forcing one Dirichlet polynomial to satisfy incompatible length and moment demands. A polynomial of length T^(1/W) only admits useful control for O(W) moments, while shortening it worsens the log-zeta majorant; moreover, Markov bounds from moments do not reconstruct sharp large-value frequencies. Splitting the polynomial into blocks lets later, longer, lower-variance pieces be raised to smaller powers, and working directly with truncated exponential moments avoids the lossy tail-reconstruction step.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: The source identifies two losses in the earlier route: usable moments decrease as Dirichlet-polynomial length increases, and Markov-inequality tail estimates are not optimal even given moment information. It proposes A=sum_j A_j, bounds |zeta|^(2k) by the product of exp(2k Re A_j), truncates each exponential when its block is controlled, and handles a point with an oversized block using a shorter log-zeta majorant together with the small measure of such points.
directed.conceptual_reading: This is a multiscale compatibility repair. The block decomposition allocates different proof budgets to components according to their expected contribution and admissible moment order; exceptional points are localized by the first failed scale rather than making the whole approximation uniformly short. Direct exponential-moment control also preserves the quantity ultimately needed instead of passing through an insufficient tail summary.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The bridge is from the additive representation A=sum_j A_j to the multiplicative representation exp(2k Re A)=product_j exp(2k Re A_j). Expected block-size control makes each factor replaceable by a short polynomial, while an oversized block becomes an exceptional-set witness that licenses changing to a shorter cutoff.
directed.boundary_or_failure: This span gives the proof architecture, not the estimates that justify the truncations, exceptional-set measures, or product integrals. It produces an upper-bound mechanism only and does not establish a sharp large-value distribution or a Gaussian limit.
directed.uncertainty: Low for the stated obstruction and repair: they are explicit in prose. Exact normalization in the displayed Dirichlet polynomials has text-layer formula risk but is not needed for this reading.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: Squaring the truncated exponential is a positivity device, not cosmetic algebra. On the good set, |Re F_i(t)| is bounded strongly enough to truncate exp(k Re F_i(t)) at a block-dependent degree with exponentially small error. Squaring that truncation keeps the product integrand nonnegative, so an integral over the good set can be enlarged safely to all of [T,2T].

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: The target integrand is written as product_i (exp(k Re F_i(t)))^2. The good-set bound |Re F_i(t)| <= beta_i^(-3/4) permits truncation at degree about 100k beta_i^(-3/4), with error O(exp(-100k beta_i^(-3/4))). The resulting finite sum is squared, and positivity then justifies replacing the integration domain by [T,2T] in an upper bound.
directed.conceptual_reading: The representation is chosen to preserve an order property through approximation. A direct truncation of exp(2k Re F_i) would approximate the value but would not supply the same manifest nonnegativity after truncation; splitting the exponent and squaring makes domain enlargement compatible with the desired inequality.
directed.representation_or_bridge: A bounded analytic exponential is converted into a short squared Dirichlet-polynomial expression. The square is a positivity certificate that bridges local good-set control to global mean-value integration, where orthogonality can later be applied.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The construction only applies where all block values satisfy the good-set bounds. This unit does not estimate the expanded full-interval integral or treat bad strata; those require the later pairing and exceptional-set arguments.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The expanded positive truncations are kept short enough that time integration becomes a prime-multiplicity test. The geometric block scales and block-dependent degrees force the total prime product below a small power of T, allowing Proposition 2 to replace the cosine integral by T times a nonnegative square-supported function f plus a negligible error. Multiplicativity then reassembles the many indices into independent block factors.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: After expanding both squares and every block polynomial, the product of all participating primes is bounded by T^0.1 using the geometric beta_i progression, the truncation degrees, and the small terminal beta_I. Proposition 2 evaluates each cosine-product integral as T f(product)+O(T^0.1). Since f is nonnegative, the original weighted coefficients C are dominated by reciprocal-square-root coefficients D. The accumulated error is bounded by T^0.2 (log log T)^(2k), and multiplicativity of f converts the main sum into a product over blocks, recovering coefficients with powers of 2k.
directed.conceptual_reading: This is the deterministic realization of an independence heuristic. Short total Dirichlet length makes oscillatory time integration act like an orthogonality filter; f records exactly the surviving even-multiplicity configurations. Disjoint prime blocks and multiplicativity then expose a product structure analogous to independent increments without assuming probabilistic independence.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The proof passes from an analytic integral of products of cosines to a combinatorial sum indexed by prime tuples, with f as the bridge object encoding square support. It then uses coefficient domination and multiplicativity to compress that tuple sum back into blockwise products. The domination forgets some smooth weights in exchange for a tractable upper bound.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The step depends on Proposition 2 and on the verified short-length inequality. Replacing C by D and estimating the error are one-sided losses. This unit stops before evaluating the square-supported multiplicities; that collapse occurs in the next unit.
directed.uncertainty: The qualitative reduction and the T^0.1/T^0.2 bounds are clear, but the dense extracted products and multi-indices carry high formula-layout risk; exact reuse should retain the checked span or scan.

Their ratio reduces the block contribution to terms k^(2n)/(n! p_1...p_n product_j alpha_j!). directed.boundary_or_failure: This is an upper bound, not a proof that the prime sum is Gaussian or that zeta has a limiting Gaussian distribution. spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The conjectural constant is decomposed into two structurally different factors: an arithmetic Euler product a(k) and a random-matrix gamma-product limit f(k). Their large-k decays, respectively exp(-k^2 log log k+O(k^2)) and exp(-k^2 log k+O(k^2)), predict a combined scale dramatically smaller than the proof's double-exponential constant.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: The Keating-Snaith prediction is stated as the fixed-k asymptotic integral_0^T |zeta(1/2+it)|^(2k) dt asymptotic to a(k) f(k) T (log T)^(k^2). The span defines a(k) by an Euler product and f(k) by a limit of gamma-function products. It records a(k)=exp(-k^2 log log k+O(k^2)) and f(k)=exp(-k^2 log k+O(k^2)) as k grows, hence a(k)f(k)<=exp(-k^2 log k) for large fixed k.
directed.conceptual_reading: Factorizing the conjectural constant separates local arithmetic effects from the global random-matrix contribution. Their asymptotic scales serve as a quantitative diagnostic for where a rigorous upper-bound method is losing information, rather than merely saying its constant is large.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The Euler product packages prime-local multiplicities, while the gamma-product limit packages the matrix-model contribution. Their product is the comparison bridge between zeta moments and the conjectural random-matrix model.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The asymptotic and its factors are conjectural in this span, not proved by the conditional moment upper bound. The fixed-k limit T to infinity and the subsequent large-k discussion must not be conflated with a uniform two-parameter theorem; the displayed inequality is only a coarse benchmark.
directed.uncertainty: The roles and stated large-k scales are clear, but the exact Euler/gamma formulas are extraction-sensitive and should be retained with the source display.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: Optimizing the polynomial length turns the constant mismatch into a precise missing estimate. Modeling the prime polynomial of length x as Gaussian gives a majorant cost exp(2k log T/log x) and a variance reward exp(k^2 log log x). Balancing them selects log x=2 log T/k, or x=T^(2/k), and recovers the conjectural exp(-k^2 log k+O(k^2)) scale; the rigorous bad-block lemma cannot handle that length.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: For log^2 T<=x<=T^2, Proposition 1 gives a log-zeta upper bound whose deterministic penalty contributes exp(2k(log T/log x+O(1))). The source heuristically treats the accompanying prime sum as mean-zero Gaussian with variance (1/2)log log x+O(1), so its exponential moment is exp(k^2(log log x+O(1))). Minimizing exp(2k log T/log x+k^2 log log x) gives log x=2 log T/k and the bound exp(-k^2 log k+O(k^2)) T (log T)^(k^2). Making this rigorous would require Lemma 2 control for Dirichlet polynomials of length T^(2/k), which the author cannot obtain.
directed.conceptual_reading: The heuristic is valuable as an obstruction finder: a free representation parameter, polynomial length, is optimized in the surrogate Gaussian model, and the optimizer identifies exactly which analytic capacity the rigorous architecture lacks. Agreement with the random-matrix scale is evidence that the diagnosed length is meaningful, not proof of the conjecture.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The log-zeta majorant bridges zeta moments to a prime polynomial plus a length penalty; the Gaussian moment-generating function compresses the prime polynomial to its variance; optimization then bridges the conjectural constant to the concrete target x=T^(2/k).
directed.boundary_or_failure: The calculation explicitly neglects zeros, treats the prime polynomial as Gaussian, and handles small primes too generously, so it does not recover the arithmetic factor a(k). It is conjectural, assumes the stated x range and T sufficiently large relative to k, and ends at an unavailable long-polynomial estimate rather than a proof.
directed.uncertainty: Low for the optimizer and stated obstruction, which are explicit. Medium for exact displayed normalizations and O(1) terms because the formulas are extraction-dependent.
